newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels say won't accept truce before talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels say won't accept truce before talks.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Saturday rebels could accept a five-point U.N. plan as a basis for more discussions but a ceasefire could only come after talks.
Kabila said his forces were within 50 km (30 miles) of Kisangani, the biggest city in northeast Zaire, and advancing from several directions.

But he told a news conference in the eastern Zairean border city of Goma his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) was meeting heavy resistance from former Rwandan Armed Forces (FAR) troops as they pushed for Kisangani.
Kabila said the rebels could accept the U.N. peace plan, which Kinshasa only agreed to under the pressure of rebel advances, but only as the basis for talks before any ceasefire.
"If we accept it then it is so that we can negotiate, the points on the plan are there for discussions," Kabila said.
An immediate ceasefire is the first point of the U.N. peace plan, which the U.N. Security Council adopted on February 18 and on Friday urged Kabila's rebels to accept and stop fighting.

France, which has backed President Mobutu Sese Seko and called for international military intervention in Zaire, said on Saturday if a ceasefire failed to take effect the council should meet again to "study necessary measures".
Kabila has said he would only negotiate with Mobutu and only over how he will step down. The 66-year-old president is in Europe where he had surgery for prostate cancer last year.
"We will negotiate the ceasefire with the Mobutists and there are no pre-conditions," said Kabila, 56.
Since launching their rebellion in October to topple Mobutu, the rebels have won control of at least a sixth of Zaire and are poised to assault Kisangani and its airport, a military base.

"Around Kisangani there are still problems," Kabila said. "There is a strong defence from the ex-FAR. The ex-FAR are the ones who are fighting and they have new arms and uniforms from somewhere...the Zairean soldiers are already coming over to our side."
"We are holding our positions and moving forwards in all directions," he said, adding if the airport at Kisangani was mined his rebels would clear them.

"People in Kinshasa must come out and demonstrate against the power of (Prime Minister) Kengo wa Dondo and the others and refuse to be slaves in their own country," said Kabila, the most successful rebel leader against Mobutu's 31 year-old rule.
With the rebels advancing in the east and south and meeting little resistance from the army, more and more people in the vast Central African country now apparently back kabila.
Zaire's main opposition party accused soldiers on Saturday of mistreating seven of its leaders and militants detained for trying to march in Kinshasa in support of talks with the rebels.
Troops intervened on Friday to stop the party militants demonstrating to demand peace talks between Kabila and Mobutu.

Raphael Ngenda, AFDL information minister, earlier denied unconfirmed reports of massacres of Rwandan refugees by rebels. The Security Council on Friday referred to the reports by noting allegations of violations of international humanitarian law.
"If there have been killings then they are by the (Rwandan) Hutu extremists themselves who have killed their own brothers (refugees) to stop them going home," Ngenda told Reuters.
U.N. officials said Martin Griffiths, U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the Great Lakes region of central Africa, would lead a U.N. mission by plane on Sunday to Tingi Tingi in Zaire.
Some 170,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees abandoned Tingi Tingi camp, 210 km (130 miles) southeast of Kisangani, on February 28, shortly before it was overrun by rebel forces.
The U.N. World Food Programme said it began on Saturday giving food to between 10,000 and 20,000 refugees and displaced Zaireans in Ubundu, 130 km (80 miles) northwest of Tingi Tingi.
